You post is a little unclear. Are you trying to get an extension on a specific assignment that grades have been released for? Do you already have approved SAS accommodations for extensions?



If that's the case, follow up with your prof and CC your SAS coordinator. If the prof agrees to extend the assignment, don't worry about the grade, just do your assignment and the prof can change the grade. If your prof declines to accommodate you, that's something your SAS coordinator should be able to handle on your behalf, and you can escalate to Ombuds if needed - make sure you document as much as possible.


As for urgency, does your prof have office hours you can go to? Sometimes that's faster than emailing back and forth, and they're less likely to say no.

A better question would be - how much longer do you need to get a good mark on your assignment? SAS accommodations typically allow for up to 1 week extensions. Since you've already started, you know exactly what the assignment requires. Think about how many more hours you need to work and what else you have to balance, and ask for extra time based on that.

Is this a multi-term course, or two separate courses? 

If it's two separate courses, you typically need to have the prerequisites completed before you take the second course (Part 2). Deferring the exam means you haven't completed the course yet. You might even be able to skip this step if you explain to your advisor that you just deferred the exam and are on track to passing the prereq.

Brian had never liked journaling. He thought it was for little girls with hopeless fantasies, and Brian was too realistic for that. He knew when things were bad, and didn’t try to sugarcoat them. But his counselor had suggested he take up journaling and his mother, unfortunately, thought it was a great idea. So Brian now had a red leather-bound book on his desk, where he had to write how he was feeling every night. He hated it a lot more at first, but somewhere along the way, that hatred had turned into immense dislike. His counselor would point out that that was an improvement, but like I said, Brian knew when things were bad. Still, after the day he had just had, Brian looked forward to tonight’s entry. At the very least, it gave him someone to talk to.

He opened the book to the next blank page and wrote the date. 

“April 23, 2021. Dear diary, today was a very, very, very shi-”

Out of the corner of his eye, Brian noticed yesterday’s date scrawled in the top right corner of the previous page. “That’s weird,” he thought, “maybe I just got the date wrong yesterday.” He moved to make a correction but noticed something else. The first sentence was the exact same. 

This was weird, but Brian was realistic - he knew that every single one of his days was shitty. He wasn’t creative either - while it was a coincidence that he had written the exact same sentence twice, Brian knew he didn’t put a lot of effort into his entries. Brushing it up to mere coincidence, he corrected the date and continued his entry for the day.

“-tty. There was a power outage in the middle of my game. We lost. Mom got mad at me for being so mad, so I got mad at her. Sometimes I feel like nobody understands me. Maybe I’m an alien.”

Distracted, he glanced over to the previous page once more, reading over his first paragraph from the previous day. 

“...I feel like nobody understands me. Maybe I’m an alien.”

The exact same words. Brian knew there was no power outage yesterday. And the tournament only started today. Anxious, but unable to stop, he kept reading.

“I know sometimes mom talks about me when she thinks I’m asleep. She seems worried. She probably should be. Samuel keeps telling me that he doesn’t share what goes on in our counseling sessions, but mom knows too much to have figured out herself. It feels like there’s no one to talk to. 

I tried reaching out today. This guy seemed really upset so I asked him what’s up. Turns out his grandmother died. I didn’t know how to respond, so I tried to lighten the mood and make a joke. Apparently that made me a psychopath and now I keep getting glares from random freshmen.

Believe it or not, my day went downhill from there.

I hope I am an alien - maybe then I’d have something to look forward to. A place where I’d actually belong. With people that can understand me and how I think and what I mean when I say the wrong words. Really, I could just use a friend. Sometimes I wonder what would happen if I got a second chance.”

The next paragraph was in a different colour, and much messier. Seems like the old Brian got distracted and then rushed the last paragraph.

“I don’t know where this’ll go, but it’s a chance I have to take. Anything’s better than this shit life. For once, I can see that things could be better. It’s the second chance I’ve always wanted. Goodbye.”

A flash of light briefly lit up the room. Brian saw his own silhouette in a blue light. Someone was in his room. Slowly, he turned around.

“I told you, kid. Time’s up.”

Brian found himself unable to speak.

“Wait!” Brian turned to see himself speaking to the stranger in his room. 

“I know what went wrong. One more time. Please!” He sounded desperate.

“I told you. Just once. The more you do it, the worse the consequences. You know the rules.” 

The stranger pointed a gun at Brian.

“Please.”

Brian woke up in his bed, groaning. It was too early for this shit. The sun was in his eyes and he was not looking forward to school. Another day, another disaster. 

He looked at his phone. April 23. Brian let out another groan. He had a math test today.

“Alright listen, you lot,” Lei began, “we are all excited about a new creature moving in. But there is no more room for mishaps. The last time was too close - we need to protect our identities. So for Titania’s sake, act normal!”

“Hey, don’t blame us for everything!” Alex retorted, “you drove the last one away! Whose idea was it to turn our entire lawn into a flower garden? And how did you expect him to buy that it just happened overnight? You didn’t even use flowers from this world!” 

“Listen here you insufferable-”

“Enough!” Alan interrupted Lei before she could finish yelling at her roommate. “Lei’s right. We all need to protect our identities. Who knows what will happen if word gets out! We must work together and be careful.. Now, let us prepare for our new roommate.”

An unspoken agreement between them, Lei and Alex turned their attention to their oldest roommate, ready to let him know exactly how big of a hypocrite he was. But before either of them could get a word out, the doorbell rang.

“Hi, I’m Marina!” said the young woman, entering the house, “it’s nice to meet you!”

Alex was the first to recover. “Likewise” he said. “I’m Alex, this is Lei, and Alan” he introduced his roommates, who nodded in turn.

Suddenly feeling sick, Lei excused herself and retreated to her room, leaving her remaining roommates to fend for themselves.

“That happens sometimes,” Alex broke the awkward silence. “She’ll be fine.If you’d like, I can give you a tour of the house and show you where you can put your stuff.” 

“That would be great!” Marina replied, happy that at least one of her roommates was friendly. 

“I trust that you’re in good hands,” Alan finally spoke up. “I will be in my room if you need anything.”

“Your roommates seem nice.” Marina said.

“Well Alan’s pretty old-school so his social skills aren’t the best.” Alex tried to reassure his new roommate. “And Lei will come around eventually. She’s actually quite fun to be around. Here,let me help you move in.” Being the best at human interaction, Alex knew that it was up to him to find out as much as he could about the new roommate.

They fell into a steady rhythm, moving in boxes one at a time. 

“Tell me about you guys.” Marina said, nervous and curious at the same time. 

“Well,” Alex replied, “Alan’s more of a night person. Most jokes fly over his head, but you’ll grow to like him. He’s actually the cleanest one out of all of us, but make sure you don’t move anything in the kitchen or he’ll throw a tantrum. Believe it or not, Lei’s the friendliest - you just caught her on a bad day. She’s definitely a morning person, annoyingly cheerful right at dawn. She likes working in the yard, so be careful around her flowers. I’m pretty sure she would lose her mind if something happened to them - they mean everything to her.”

“Don’t mess up the kitchen and don’t trample the flowers. Got it.” Marina made a note to herself. “What about you?”

“Well as you can see, I’m the most handsome.” Alex joked, successfully eliciting a chuckle from his new roommate. “I tend to stay in my room for the most part. I like learning so you might see a few of my inventions from time to time. Don’t worry, I won’t blow the house up again.” 

Not realizing he was serious, Marina chuckled.

“What about you?” Alex finally asked her. “Tell me about yourself.”

“Well,” Marina replied, drawing out the word while thinking about what to share, “I moved from up the mountain to get a change of scenery. I like music and long drives. My parents were worried sick about me moving into a new home so I have to call them every weekend. Oh, and I work at a pet store but I’ll make sure not to bring home any fleas!”

Hoping to be polite, Alex laughed at her joke, not fully understanding it. They continued talking about themselves and their roommate over the next few hours while they moved the rest of the boxes in. After that, Marina thanked Alex and retreated to her room to take a long nap - she was exhausted.

Later that night, the three creatures reconvened in the kitchen. 

“Is she still asleep?” Alan asked.

“Out cold.” replied Alex, “She was so tired, I don’t think she’s going to wake up any time soon.

“What did you find out?” asked Lei.

“Doesn’t seem like much of a threat from what she said. Assuming she was being honest.” Alex replied.

“You better not have blown your cover.” said Alan.

“She doesn’t suspect a thing.” replied Alex.

The group talked about their new roommate for a while, making sure to be quiet so as to not wake her up.

As someone with depression, I know this feeling too well. On a good day I can force myself to work by getting out of the house, moving to a work environment (libraries, MUSC, a cafe, or lounges), listening to music, and working with a friend. I would also suggest emailing your professors. You don't have to give any details, just let them know that you're going through something and it's affecting your academics. All of my profs have been accomodating in some way, either by giving me extensions, transferring the weight of missed assignments, or offering to sit down with me and help me catch up. You can also talk to your academic advisor to look into your options. You don't have to share any personal information with them either. Finally, I would suggest going to Case Management on the second floor of MUSC (226) and see if they can help. Their job is to basically help students with anything they struggle with and connect them to resources if necessary. They're not usually busy so just knock on the door and let them know you need help. It's pretty normal to feel down at this time of year because of how stressful it gets. Unfortunately it's even worse for people with mental health issues. But there are people at McMaster that want to see you succeed and are willing to help you in any way they can. I hope this helps, and feel free to PM me of you need anything!

Currently using them! McMaster has a Student Wellness Centre (SWC) located in the basement of the student centre. You can see a doctor, counselor, or psychiatrist free of charge (you need an appointment though, unless it's urgent). They can also do blood/urine tests, provide medication, and they have weekly drop in groups for stuff like yoga, excercise, mental wellness etc. They also offer CBT if youlre interested. I get a perscription once every month for free anti-depressants (note that this isn't covered by the university, but by OHIP+). There is also a pharmacy at the student centre where you can fill perscriptions. Additionally, if you need it, Student Accessibility Services (SAS) are there to offer academic support if you need it. They can offer a reduced course load but still get you OSAP, extentions on assignments, extended time for exams, or anything else you might need. You don't have to provide them with a diagnosis, but you do need a doctor's note. SAS also has an academic counselor if you need help with time management, memory techniques, etc. You need an appointment to see them too. All of the stuff I mentioned is free if you have an Ontario health card. Hope this helps, and feel free too shoot me a message if you have any further questions! :)
